opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most tempting and most dangerous things for an early-stage company. When you're still searching for product-market fit, a big customer showing up with a real budget feels like validation, and honestly, sometimes it is. Cash in the bank buys you time, and time is the thing a startup is always running out of.

But the trap is that a large contract can quietly turn you into a consulting shop. The customer has very specific needs, they're paying you, so naturally you build what they ask for. Six months later you look up and realize your roadmap has been written by one company, and what you've built is a custom solution that maybe nobody else wants. You've optimized for one point instead of finding the general shape of the problem.

So the way I think about it is: does this contract push us toward the product we believe in, or away from it? If the customer's problem is a sharp, demanding version of something many people will need, that's great. They become a forcing function, they stress-test your technology, and you get feedback you'd never get from small users. If instead most of the work is integration, one-off features, or things you'd never ship to anyone else, you have to be very honest that you're selling engineering hours, not a product.

A few practical things help. Be explicit, internally and with the customer, about what stays in the core product and what's custom. Keep a small team on the contract work so it doesn't swallow everyone. And set a time box, so you're deliberately revisiting whether it's still aligned instead of drifting.

In our own experience building developer tools and infrastructure, the hardest part isn't saying yes or no, it's staying disciplined after you say yes. Revenue is addictive. The real question is whether, a year later, you'll have something that's reusable, scalable, and closer to what the broader market needs, or just a happy customer and a product that hasn't moved.

r001.rationale: The response warns that large contracts can divert a startup into custom consulting work during product-market-fit search, but it does not identify taking work outside the startup’s strengths as the complication.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, this is one of the hardest tensions we've dealt with at Taichi, and I don't think there's a clean answer. When you're still figuring out product-market fit, a big customer showing up with a contract feels like validation, and it's real money. But I've learned to be very careful about it.

The thing is, a large-customer contract is often a disguised consulting engagement. They have a very specific problem, and they want you to solve that problem, not build a product. If you take it, you can easily spend six months building features that exactly one company needs. You get paid, but you come out the other side with a product that's shaped like that customer's org chart instead of like the market.

So the way I think about it now is to ask a few questions before saying yes. First, does the work they want pull us toward where we already believe the product should go, or away from it? If it's on the roadmap anyway, then great, someone is paying us to build it faster, and we get a real user giving us real feedback. That's the best case. Second, how much of the work is generalizable? If eighty percent of it ends up in the core product and twenty percent is custom glue, that's fine. If it's the reverse, that's a trap. And third, what does the engagement do to the team's attention? A small team can really only hold one thing in its head at a time. If the contract consumes the people who should be talking to twenty different users, you've traded learning for revenue, and early on, learning is usually worth more.

There's also a subtler cost. A big customer tends to make you feel like you've found product-market fit when you haven't. One company loving you is not a market. I've seen teams, including us at moments, mistake one strong signal for a pattern and then over-invest in that direction.

That said, I wouldn't say never. When we were working with early users doing physics simulation and graphics, some of the most important technical decisions came out of a very demanding user pushing on a specific workload. Demanding users teach you things that casual users never will. The key is to structure it so you keep control of the product direction. Scope it tightly, keep the timeline short, make it clear what you will and won't build, and be willing to walk away if it becomes a custom development shop.

So my answer is, take it if it's aligned and bounded, and treat it as a paid experiment rather than as the business. The moment it starts to define the business, that's when you've lost the plot on finding fit.

r001.rationale: The response warns that customer-specific consulting can distract from the product and market learning, but it does not identify taking on work outside the startup’s strengths as the complication.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to be careful, because a large customer can give you revenue without necessarily giving you product-market fit. You might end up building something very specific for them, and then discover that nobody else needs it.

The question I would ask is: if we build this, will it make the product more useful for other customers we want to serve? If the answer is yes, the contract can be a great opportunity to learn, with someone paying for that development. But if it takes the whole team in a different direction, you have to account for that opportunity cost.

So I wouldn’t reject contract work categorically. I would keep the scope clear and make sure we’re learning about a repeatable customer need. The goal is to build a product we can sell again, rather than have every new customer become a new project.

r001.rationale: The response warns that customer-specific work can distract the team and fail to address a repeatable need, but it does not identify work outside the startup’s strengths as the complication.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is whether the work helps you discover a product that other customers will also want. A large customer can give you a very concrete problem, and that’s valuable when you’re still figuring out product-market fit. But the contract itself isn’t proof that you’ve found it.

If you’re building something very specific to their organization, you can end up spending all your time serving one customer. So I’d ask: if this customer disappeared tomorrow, would we still want to build this? Could we sell the same capability to someone else?

If the answer is yes, the contract can fund useful product development. If the answer is no, you should recognize that you’re taking on consulting work and be deliberate about how much of the team’s time you commit to it.

r001.rationale: The response warns against work tailored to one customer and recommends recognizing consulting commitments, but it does not identify taking on work outside the startup’s strengths as an avoidable complication.
